title: 1991 AHSME Problem 13
statement: Horses \(X,\) \(Y,\) and \(Z\) are entered in a three-horse race in which ties are not possible. If the odds against \(X\) winning are \(3\)-to-\(1\) and the odds against \(Y\) winning are \(2\)-to-\(3,\) what are the odds against \(Z\) winning? (By “odds against \(H\) winning are \(p\)-to-\(q\)” we mean that the probability of \(H\) winning the race is \(\frac{q}{p+q}.\))

solutions.text:
The given probabilities are \(P(X)=\frac14\) and \(P(Y)=\frac35.\) Therefore \[ P(Z)=1-\frac14-\frac35=\frac3{20}. \] The probability that \(Z\) loses is \(\frac{17}{20},\) so the odds against \(Z\) are \(17\)-to-\(3.\)

Thus the correct answer is D.
hints: Convert each set of odds to a probability
The three winning probabilities sum to \(1\)
